paragraphs.context: Want to know what the most fantastically radical game ever is?
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks if you want to know the greatest, coolest game ever.

paragraphs.context: My best buddies – Quint, June, and Dirk – are racing through town in
paragraphs.simple: His friends race through town in bumper cars that they made stronger and faster. They call them BoomKarts.

paragraphs.context: Dirk built the BoomKarts, and Quint loaded ’em up with wicked vehicular
paragraphs.simple: Dirk built the karts, and Quint added fun weapons: paint guns, marbles to drop behind them, tyres with spikes and more.

background.note: A game where you shoot balls of paint at other players.

paragraphs.context: But me, Jack Sullivan? I don’t need a BoomKart because I race
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not need a kart. He rides his monster-dog, Rover.

paragraphs.context: There’s a reason for this game of Real-Life Super Mario Kart.
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw that his friends were tired and bored. They looked almost like zombies.

paragraphs.context: So I was like, ‘WE NEED EXCITEMENT!
paragraphs.simple: So Jack made a big race course through town, with jumps, oily places and a path through an old man's house.

background.note: A small, low car for racing.

paragraphs.context: That’s one of the perks of life after the Monster Apocalypse – you
paragraphs.mainIdea: A good thing about the end of the world.
paragraphs.simple: After the Monster Apocalypse, you can build a huge race track through your own town.

paragraphs.context: Right now, June’s winning, and I must take her out!
paragraphs.simple: June has won three races in a row. Jack takes out his T-shirt cannon to stop her.

paragraphs.context: Direct hit! June’s kart slices around the corner, spins, then slams into
paragraphs.simple: The shot hits June. Her kart spins and crashes into the fire station.

paragraphs.context: ‘Don’t mess with the king!’ I shout. Rover woofs triumphantly as we
paragraphs.simple: Jack shouts that he is the king and takes first place. Then he sees that June's kart is badly broken.

paragraphs.context: Crud. The idea is to win, not to knock your buddies unconscious
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to win, but he does not want to hurt his friends.

paragraphs.context: THWACK! The football knocks me clean out of Rover’s saddle. I fall
paragraphs.simple: A football from June's kart knocks Jack off Rover. He falls on the grass.

paragraphs.context: ‘Your problem, Jack, is that you’re too nice,’ June teases.
paragraphs.simple: June laughs and says Jack is too nice to win. She wants to win more than he does.

paragraphs.context: And I don’t use the term ‘INSANE’ lightly, since pretty much everything
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not call things "insane" easily, because almost everything after the Monster Apocalypse is crazy.

paragraphs.context: I can’t make out the words, but the voice is coming from
paragraphs.mainIdea: A voice from the fire station.
paragraphs.simple: They have not seen or heard any other people since the Monster Apocalypse started. Now a voice comes from the fire station.

paragraphs.context: June looks at me, eyes bulging. CONFIRMED: this is both INSANE and BONKERS BANANAS.
paragraphs.simple: June looks at Jack with wide eyes. They both think this is amazing.

paragraphs.context: ‘No way, friend!’ Quint shouts as his BoomKart whips around the corner
paragraphs.simple: Quint thinks Jack is playing a trick to stop the race, like before.

paragraphs.context: June points out that I should not be yelling, since we have
paragraphs.simple: June says Jack should not shout, because they do not know who is inside. Jack thinks of all the bad things it could be.

paragraphs.context: Tyres screech, and Quint and Dirk skid to a stop and hop
paragraphs.simple: Quint and Dirk stop their karts and jump out.

paragraphs.context: ‘Of course you’re curious!’ I say. ‘We haven’t heard a single other
paragraphs.simple: Jack is excited. They have heard monster voices, but no other human voices for months.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, my mind is in a whole different place, thinking about how
paragraphs.simple: Jack starts worrying that his own voice sounds funny, through his nose. Maybe that is why he had few friends before.

paragraphs.context: ‘Jack!’ June snaps me back to attention, hooking a thumb at the
paragraphs.simple: June stops Jack's thinking and points at the door. Dirk opens it.

paragraphs.context: ‘Watch out!’ June cries. A hefty undead fire chief is swiping at Quint!
paragraphs.simple: A big zombie fire chief attacks Quint.

paragraphs.context: Quint immediately curls up into a ball and plays dead like it’s
paragraphs.simple: Quint lies still like you should with a bear. Dirk grabs two zombies by their feet and throws them, because he is very strong.

paragraphs.context: We hurry inside the station before the other zombies can get their
paragraphs.simple: They run into the station before more zombies come. Rover just fits through the door, and Jack shuts it.

paragraphs.context: The fire station is chilly, and the whole place smells like rotted
paragraphs.simple: The station is cold and smells of dead bodies, old food and old cheese sandwiches.

background.note: Long bread rolls with hot meat and cheese inside.

paragraphs.context: So who did we just hear talking?
paragraphs.simple: Zombies do not talk; they only moan. So who did they hear?

paragraphs.context: We soon determine that there is no one else – zombie or non
paragraphs.simple: They look in every room. There is no one else in the station.

paragraphs.context: Capital letters ‘IT’ ’cause IT is BIG.
paragraphs.simple: Jack writes "IT" in capital letters because it is so important.

paragraphs.context: We hear the voice. It’s coming from a radio .
paragraphs.simple: The voice comes from a radio.

paragraphs.context: My heart just about seizes up and my blood starts pumping to

sentences.context: June’s kart slices around the corner, spins, then slams into the local fire station.
sentences.simple: June's kart goes fast around the corner, turns round and round, and then crashes into the fire station.
sentences.main: June's kart slams into the fire station.

parts.meaning: June's small car
moves very fast around the corner,
turns round and round,

parts.text: then slams into the local fire station.
parts.meaning: and then hits the town's fire station hard.

sentences.grammar: Three verbs in the present tense tell the actions one after another: "slices", "spins", "slams". Commas and "then" join them. "Slice" here means move fast and smoothly, like a knife.

sentences.context: The sound of pained scraping fills my ears while dread floods my stomach.
sentences.simple: Jack hears the terrible sound of Rover being dragged, and he feels very afraid.
sentences.main: The sound fills my ears.

parts.meaning: The sound of something hurt being dragged
is all I can hear
and at the same time a strong fear fills my stomach.

sentences.grammar: "While" joins two things that happen at the same time. "Floods" is used in a picture way: the fear comes in fast, like water.

sentences.context: There’s something in his chilling eyes and dripping fangs that resembles a sly smile.
sentences.simple: The monster's cold eyes and wet teeth look almost like a clever, unkind smile.
sentences.main: Something resembles a sly smile.

parts.meaning: There is something

parts.text: in his chilling eyes and dripping fangs
parts.meaning: in his frightening eyes and wet, sharp teeth
that looks like a clever, tricky smile.

sentences.grammar: "There's something ... that ..." is a way to start talking about a thing you notice. "That resembles" tells more about "something".

sentences.context: Soon, we will be able to listen to whoever is talking out there.
sentences.simple: Quint says that soon they will hear the people who are talking on the radio.
sentences.main: We will be able to listen.

parts.meaning: In a short time,

parts.text: we will be able to listen
parts.meaning: we will be able to hear

parts.text: to whoever is talking out there.
parts.meaning: any person who is talking somewhere out in the world.

sentences.grammar: "Will be able to" is the future of "can". "Whoever" = any person who; we do not know who it is.

sentences.context: I’m checking the date on our calendar when I come up with a plan.
sentences.simple: Jack is looking at the calendar when he suddenly thinks of a plan.
sentences.main: I come up with a plan.

parts.text: I’m checking the date on our calendar
parts.meaning: I am looking at the date on our calendar

parts.text: when I come up with a plan.
parts.meaning: when I suddenly think of a plan.

sentences.grammar: "I'm checking" (present continuous) is the longer action; "when I come up with" (present simple) is the short thing that happens in the middle of it. "Come up with" = think of.

sentences.context: I never should have let the Helidrone be used in the games.
sentences.simple: Jack is sorry that he let his flying toy be used in the games.
sentences.main: I never should have let it.

parts.meaning: It was a mistake to
allow the Helidrone (his toy helicopter)
to be used in the games.

sentences.grammar: "Should have + past participle" talks about the past: it was a mistake, and you are sorry now. "Let + something + be used" = allow others to use it.

sentences.context: How could I let all this come to an end?
sentences.simple: Jack asks himself how he could allow this happy life to finish.
sentences.main: How could I let this end?

parts.meaning: How was it possible for me to
allow everything here
finish?

sentences.grammar: This is a question that does not need an answer: Jack means "I must not let this end." "Let + something + verb" = allow it to happen.

sentences.context: What is it about me that got the King Wretch’s attention?
sentences.simple: Jack wonders why the King Wretch is interested in him.
sentences.main: What got its attention?

parts.meaning: What thing about me is it

parts.text: that got the King Wretch’s attention?
parts.meaning: that made the King Wretch notice me?

sentences.grammar: "What is it about X that ...?" asks which part or quality of X is the reason for something.

sentences.context: Normally, Big Mama is a classic monster-battling vehicle with gadgets and weapons galore.

parts.meaning: Usually,

parts.text: Big Mama is a classic monster-battling vehicle
parts.meaning: Big Mama is a very good car for fighting monsters
with very many clever machines and weapons.

sentences.grammar: "Galore" comes after the noun and means "very many". "Monster-battling" is one adjective made from two words: a vehicle that battles monsters.

parts.meaning: Naturally

parts.text: I’ve never been on a waterbed
parts.meaning: I have never been on a bed filled with water

parts.text: because waterbeds are for cool dudes.
parts.meaning: because only cool people have waterbeds.

sentences.grammar: "I've never been" (present perfect) talks about your whole life up to now. "Because" gives the reason. Jack is laughing at himself.

sentences.simple: Jack feels so nervous that he must leave the tree house quickly.
sentences.main: I need to get out.

parts.text: I need to get out of this tree house
parts.meaning: I must leave this tree house
before my heart explodes like a bomb.

sentences.grammar: "Before" + present tense can talk about the future. "My heart detonates" is a funny way to say "I feel very, very nervous."

sentences.context: I might be doing a lot of things by myself.
sentences.simple: Jack thinks that soon he may have to do many things alone.

parts.meaning: Maybe I will be doing
many things
alone.

sentences.grammar: "Might be + -ing" talks about something that is possible in the future. "By myself" = alone, with no one else.

sentences.context: We step over the crumpled gate, and we’re there, inside Fun Land.

parts.text: We step over the crumpled gate,
parts.meaning: We walk over the bent, broken gate,
and we have arrived,
in Fun Land.

sentences.grammar: Jack tells the story in the present tense to make it feel exciting. "Inside Fun Land" explains "there".

sentences.simple: Jack is afraid that all his friends' hard work will be lost.
sentences.main: Everything will be ruined.

parts.meaning: All the things

parts.text: my friends worked so hard for
parts.meaning: that my friends worked very hard to get
will be destroyed.

sentences.grammar: "My friends worked so hard for" tells more about "everything"; the word "that" is left out. "Will be ruined" is the future passive.

sentences.context: If I can’t, then they won’t be able to get the radio working.
sentences.simple: If Jack cannot keep the monster busy, his friends cannot fix the radio.
sentences.main: They won’t be able to get the radio working.

parts.text: then they won’t be able to
parts.meaning: then they will not be able to
make the radio work.

sentences.grammar: This is a first conditional: "If + present, ... will/won't". "Get something working" = make it work.

sentences.context: They’d better get that radio fixed, or this was all for nothing.
sentences.simple: Jack hopes his friends fix the radio, or everything he did was useless.
sentences.main: They’d better get that radio fixed.

parts.meaning: They really must
have that radio repaired,

parts.text: or this was all for nothing.
parts.meaning: or all of this was useless.

sentences.grammar: "'d better" = "had better": a strong way to say "should". "Get something fixed" = make sure it is repaired. "For nothing" = with no good result.

sentences.context: Growing up an orphan, I was raised by these heroes, in a way.
sentences.simple: Jack had no parents, so in a way the heroes in comics and films brought him up.

parts.meaning: Because I grew up without parents,

parts.text: I was raised by these heroes,
parts.meaning: these heroes brought me up,
not really, but almost.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part at the start ("Growing up an orphan") gives background about "I". "Was raised by" is the past passive. "In a way" = partly true.

sentences.context: Before he can finish his sentence, a flash of movement cuts through the darkness.

parts.text: Before he can finish his sentence,
parts.meaning: Before he is able to finish speaking,
something moving very fast
comes quickly through the dark.

sentences.grammar: "Before" starts the time part. "A flash of movement" = a very quick movement, like a flash of light.

sentences.context: Only Biggun’s tremendous strength keeps us from being simply plucked into the sky.

sentences.grammar: "Keep someone from + -ing" = stop someone from doing or having something. "Being plucked" is passive: someone else (the King Wretch) would pull them.

sentences.context: A massive smile appears on my face as I look to the crowd.
